title: Integrating LLMs into a Two-Tier Traditional Methodology for Automated Verilog Code Generation
evidence_span: The proposed two-tier methodology combines LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation, classifiers, heuristics, simulation, and reasoning for top-down Verilog generation, then applies bottom-up code review and functional/performance checks including parallelism, critical paths, and resource sharing; the official description compares against existing Verilog/VHDL-generation methods without reporting numeric results.
problem: Natural-language-to-Verilog generation has semantic gaps and can produce functionally or structurally unsuitable hardware when generation is not coupled to evaluation.
method_or_artifact: Two-tier RAG/classifier/heuristic prompting flow with simulation, reasoning, code review, and hardware-performance checks.
workload_or_benchmark: Natural-language hardware specifications and Verilog/VHDL generation tasks; benchmark designs, simulators, synthesis targets, and correctness criteria are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Generated RTL evaluated for parallelism, critical path, and resource sharing; target FPGA/ASIC process, synthesis tools, and model sizes are unspecified.
metrics: Comparative functional and performance evaluation claimed; numeric results are not supplied
limits: No pass rate, synthesis quality, testbench coverage, prompt set, or model/tool configuration is supplied.
Combining simulation and heuristics may improve validity while adding cost and target-specific tuning.
Official description only; generated-RTL correctness and hardware quality require paper-level verification.

title: Automated Discovery, Classification, and Systematic Security Verification Methodology for Undocumented Instructions
evidence_span: The framework automates discovery, classification, and security verification of undocumented processor instructions; the official description reports 23 newly discovered instructions, 29 classified instructions, 99.8357% classifier accuracy, and tangible security implications for five instructions.
problem: Undocumented processor instructions are security risks, while existing discovery is constrained and semantic analysis and security verification remain manual and ad hoc.
method_or_artifact: Automated instruction discovery, classifier-based semantic grouping, and systematic security-verification workflow.
workload_or_benchmark: Processor instruction sets and undocumented-instruction tests; processor models, instruction corpus, class distribution, and security properties are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Processor-level instruction execution and security analysis; architecture, firmware, privilege modes, and observation interfaces are unspecified.
limits: The description omits processor identities, corpus leakage controls, class imbalance, classifier split, and definition of tangible security impact.
Discovery counts do not establish completeness, exploitability, or severity across processor families.
Official description only; findings and security claims require paper-level verification.

title: 3D-ReSAC: A Near-3D-Stacked-DRAM Processor with Area-Efficient Sequential Refresh-Skip and High-Link-Utilization Arrowmesh Communication for Fast Low-Batch LLM Inference
evidence_span: 3D-ReSAC combines a near-3D-stacked-DRAM processor, sequential refresh-skip to reduce DRAM refresh overhead, and ArrowMesh communication to improve link utilization; the official description reports 7–100% lower refresh overhead, 53–75% lower communication overhead, and 1.12–2.02x latency reduction for low-batch LLM inference.
problem: Low-batch edge LLM inference is constrained by memory bandwidth and compute, while 3D-stacked DRAM adds refresh and collective-communication overheads.
method_or_artifact: Near-memory processor with sequential refresh-skip and high-link-utilization ArrowMesh communication.
workload_or_benchmark: Low-batch LLM inference; model suite, batch sizes, sequence lengths, accuracy, and latency baseline are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Near-3D-stacked DRAM processor and high-speed links; stack organization, DRAM technology, refresh correctness, process, and thermal conditions are unspecified.
limits: Wide ranges lack workload, stack, refresh policy, and communication conditions.
Refresh skipping must preserve data integrity; area, power, thermal, and reliability costs are unspecified.
Official description only; latency and correctness claims require paper-level verification.

title: From Fluid Dynamics to Chip Design: PDE Foundation Model Address Data Bottleneck in 3D-ICs Thermal Simulation
evidence_span: PNO-Therm adapts a foundation neural operator pretrained on diverse diffusion-like PDEs to 3D-IC thermal simulation; the official description reports less than 20% of prior training data, 6–10x lower MAE at equal data, 3.5x lower GPU memory, over 3x faster training, and approximately 940x speedup over FEM across three representative designs.
problem: Per-chip thermal models trained from scratch require large datasets and fail to exploit shared structure between heat conduction and other diffusion-type PDEs.
method_or_artifact: PDE foundation neural operator pretraining followed by targeted thermal fine-tuning for 3D-IC temperature fields.
workload_or_benchmark: Thermal simulation across three representative 3D-IC designs; geometries, power maps, mesh resolution, train/test split, and FEM configuration are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: 3D-IC thermal fields modeled against finite-element-method solvers; materials, boundary conditions, GPU, and numerical precision are unspecified.
metrics: Less than 20% of prior training data
limits: The description omits absolute error, field variables, FEM hardware/time, pretraining corpus, and transfer protocol.
Speedup and accuracy depend on discretization and solver comparison boundaries; three designs do not establish broad transfer.
Official description only; thermal fidelity and extrapolation require paper-level verification.

title: Design Technology Co-Optimization for Network on Chip in High Performance CPUs at 3nm Node Using Monolithic 3D and Backside Interconnect Technologies
evidence_span: The study compares frontside 2D, monolithic frontside 3D, backside-PDN 2D, and backside-signal 2D NoC implementations using post-layout extraction of an ARM Neoverse CSS N2 tile, realistic PDN and RC modeling, and IR-drop-aware simulation; the official description reports 53%/68% lower delay, 32%/63% lower EDP, 2.1x/3.1x feasible link frequency, and 23%/35% lower NoC latency for F3D/B2D versus F2D.
problem: Long global NoC links in many-core CPUs require repeaters and vias that degrade delay and energy, motivating technology-aware interconnect co-design.
method_or_artifact: DTCO across four 2D/3D/backside-interconnect schemes with post-layout extraction, technology-dependent RC, PDN, and IR-drop-aware circuit/system simulation.
workload_or_benchmark: ARM Neoverse CSS N2 compute tile and NoC system-level evaluations across Cortex-A76 through Cortex-N2-sized clusters; traffic, link lengths, and process details are only partially specified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: 3 nm high-performance CPU clusters, monolithic 3D integration, backside power/signal routing, extracted PDN and RC characteristics.
metrics: 53% and 68% lower delay for F3D and B2D
32% and 63% lower EDP for F3D and B2D
limits: The description omits exact process stack, routing rules, traffic workloads, thermal/assembly cost, and post-layout extraction details.
Technology preference varies by core size; results are not a universal comparison of 2D, 3D, and backside integration.
Official description only; manufacturability, yield, and full-system claims require paper-level verification.
